newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Bratsk aluminium wants Ukraine supplies.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Bratsk aluminium wants Ukraine supplies.

text.p: The world's top aluminium smelter said on Thursday it was having trouble bringing a major Ukrainian raw materials plant back into its fold as a supplier.
Yuri Shlaifshtein, a board member of Russia's Bratsk primary aluminium smelter, said talks with Ukraine's Mykolayivsky alumina plant on a five-year supply contract were held up over price quarrels.
"This is one of the best plants in Europe and of course we want to work with them," he said by telephone.
The Ukrainian plant could not be reached for comment.

Smelters in Russia, the world's largest primary aluminium exporter, are keen to re-establish ties with suppliers like Mykolayivsky, since Russia's main plants are based in southern Siberia, many miles away from other alumina suppliers.
But Mykolayivsky has thrown a spanner in the works by selling instead to Tajikistan's smelter in Tursunzade. It used to sell about 90 percent of its output to Russia.

Mykolayivsky's 1996 output of alumina, the raw material used to make aluminium, fell to 960,000 tonnes from 996,000 in 1995. Twenty-eight percent of the plant is to be privatised, possibly to foreign investors,
Shlaifshtein said Russian smelters wanted long-term contracts covering about 75 percent of Mykolayivsky's output, or 660,000 tonnes. Each tonne of alumina produces roughly half a tonne of aluminium.

Industry officials have said the Ukrainian plant, formally known as the Mykolayivsky Hlynozemny Zavod, had high production costs of about $200 per tonne and was offering material at levels above market prices.

Shlaifshtein said the price quarrel was immaterial to production plans since Bratsk had already secured supplies for this year. Bratsk was not interested in an equity stake in the plant, he said, because the Ukrainian facility had too many high production costs.

Mykolayivsky, if run at capacity, could produce enough alumina to account for nearly 20 percent of Russia's 1996 primary aluminium output of 2.87 million tonnes -- a reason why Russian smelters have held on in the talks.
